summary: Specifies Generic Routing Encapsulation, a way to wrap packets of one network protocol inside packets of another, so arbitrary payloads can be carried across arbitrary delivery networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1701 defines Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), which places a packet inside a GRE header and an outer delivery protocol. The header identifies the carried protocol and can include optional fields.

questions: what is the gre header format
what is the gre protocol type field
subtitle: A general header for carrying one network protocol inside another.

tldr.problem: Separate encapsulation schemes for each protocol pairing create a large number of specialized mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: GRE adds a header that identifies the payload protocol and indicates whether optional checksum, key, sequence, or routing fields follow.
tldr.outcome: It provides a general encapsulation mechanism, while noting that a purpose-built scheme may suit some protocol pairs better.

today: RFC 1701 is an Informational memo published in October 1994. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo points to RFC 1702 for GRE over IPv4 networks.

sections.title: The Purpose of GRE
sections.content:
RFC 1701 describes a general mechanism for encapsulating an arbitrary network-layer protocol inside another network-layer protocol. Earlier proposals handled particular protocol pairs; GRE aims to provide one mechanism that can serve many pairs.

The memo says this generality may make GRE less suitable than a specialized encapsulation for a specific pairing. It does not define when packets should be encapsulated and does not address mutual encapsulation problems.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE lets one network protocol carry a packet from another protocol. A specialized encapsulation may still be more suitable for a particular pair of protocols.

sections.title: How Encapsulation Is Layered
sections.content:
The packet being carried is the payload packet. GRE adds its own header to that packet, and another protocol may then carry the resulting GRE packet across the network.

The resulting packet has three parts: the delivery-protocol header, the GRE header, and the payload packet. The delivery protocol is used to forward the outer packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender places the payload packet inside GRE, then sends the GRE packet using a delivery protocol. The receiving system removes the GRE header before forwarding the payload.

sections.title: Fields in the GRE Header
sections.content:
The first two octets contain flags and a version. The flags indicate whether a checksum, routing information, key, or sequence number is present. If either Checksum Present or Routing Present is set, both the Checksum and Offset fields appear. The version field must be 0.

The Protocol Type field identifies the payload protocol. The optional Key is a 4-octet value that a receiver may use when authenticating a source. The optional Sequence Number is an unsigned 32-bit integer that may help establish packet order. The memo leaves the algorithms for these uses outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Flags tell the receiver which optional header fields are present. The Protocol Type identifies the payload, while the key and sequence fields provide values that other mechanisms may use.

sections.title: Optional Source Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
When the Routing Present flag is set, the header carries a list of Source Route Entries. Each entry includes an address family, an offset, a length, and routing information. A null entry marks the end of the list.

A receiver checks valid optional fields and processes source-route entries according to their address family. When the route is complete, it removes the GRE header, decrements the payload's TTL if present, and forwards the payload according to its Protocol Type.
sections.plainLanguage: If routing entries are present, the receiver processes them according to their address-family rules. After that route is complete, it removes GRE and forwards the payload packet.

sections.title: Protocol Type Values
sections.content:
The Protocol Type field identifies the payload protocol. RFC 1701 gives values including IP (0800), ARP (0806), DECnet Phase IV (6003), Transparent Ethernet Bridging (6558), and Novell IPX (8137).

The memo says future protocol types must use DIX Ethernet encoding and that its table must be used for the listed historical values. It points to the assigned Ether Type list for the full set.
sections.plainLanguage: The Protocol Type value tells the receiver how to interpret the packet carried after the GRE header. RFC 1701 lists values for several payload protocols.
